"Mechanics" has three distinct meanings as a noun. Two of them are central and worth understanding deeply. All three share a common thread, which I'll explain at the end.
Meaning 1: A Major Branch of Science

Mechanics is one of the oldest and most fundamental fields in science — a branch of physics and mathematics that studies how things move, why they move, and what forces cause or change that movement.

Every time a ball rolls down a slope, a planet orbits the sun, water flows through a pipe, or an electron spins around a nucleus — some form of mechanics describes what's happening. It is the science of the physical behavior of matter and energy in motion.

The three core things mechanics deals with are:

  • Motion — how objects travel through space and time
  • Force — pushes and pulls that cause objects to start moving, stop, speed up, slow down, or change direction
  • Energy — the capacity to cause change, and how it gets transferred or transformed

Because the physical world operates very differently at different scales — from planets down to atoms — mechanics has branched into several specialized sub-fields:

Classical Mechanics (also called Newtonian Mechanics)
This is the original and most intuitive branch, built on Isaac Newton's three laws of motion. It describes the movement of everyday-sized objects: a swinging pendulum, a car braking on a road, a thrown javelin. If something is large enough to see and not moving anywhere near the speed of light, classical mechanics explains it beautifully. Within classical mechanics, there are further divisions:

  • Kinematics — describes how objects move (speed, direction, acceleration) without asking why
  • Dynamics — goes deeper and asks why — what forces are causing the motion
  • Statics — studies objects that are not moving, and why they stay in balance (e.g., why a bridge doesn't collapse)

Quantum Mechanics
This branch deals with matter and energy at the level of atoms and subatomic particles — electrons, photons, quarks. At that unimaginably tiny scale, the rules of classical mechanics completely break down, and a strange new set of rules takes over. Particles behave like waves, their exact position and speed cannot both be known at the same time, and outcomes are described in terms of probability rather than certainty. Quantum mechanics is deeply counterintuitive, but it is one of the most precisely verified theories in all of science. It underlies technologies like lasers, semiconductors, and MRI machines.

Fluid Mechanics
This branch studies how liquids and gases behave when they flow, rest, or interact with surfaces. It explains how water moves through a pipe, how an airplane wing generates lift, how blood circulates through the heart, and how weather systems form. Fluid mechanics is divided into fluid statics (fluids at rest) and fluid dynamics (fluids in motion).

Celestial Mechanics
This applies the principles of mechanics — especially classical mechanics and gravity — to the motion of planets, moons, comets, stars, and other bodies in space. It's what allows scientists to predict exactly where a spacecraft will be years after launch.

Statistical Mechanics
This branch bridges the tiny and the large. It starts from the microscopic behavior of billions of individual particles and uses statistics to explain large-scale, observable properties — like why heating a gas increases its pressure, or why ice melts at a particular temperature.

When scientists or engineers say simply "mechanics" with no qualifier, they almost always mean classical mechanics.

One grammatical note: even though "mechanics" ends in s, when it refers to the science, it is treated as a singular noun. You say: "Mechanics is a branch of physics" — not "are."
Meaning 2: How Something Works — The Practical Details

In everyday language, "the mechanics of something" means the specific, practical details of how that thing functions or operates. It refers to the inner workings — the step-by-step processes, the systems at play, the how-it-actually-works layer of something.

This meaning is not limited to machines or science. It applies to nearly anything — negotiations, stories, policies, sports, games, writing:

  • "She understood the mechanics of negotiation — when to speak, when to stay silent, when to concede a small point to win a larger one."
    → Mechanics = the specific techniques and processes involved in negotiating.
  • "Let's talk about the mechanics of how a bill becomes a law."
    → Mechanics = the step-by-step procedural details.
  • "The coach worked on fixing his pitching mechanics."
    → Mechanics = the precise physical form and technique of his throwing action.

Notice the pattern: whenever you say "the mechanics of [something]," you are pointing to the operational, practical layer — not the big idea, but the specific nuts-and-bolts of how it actually runs.

This meaning shows up in a few specific areas with a slightly specialized flavor:

In writing and grammar: "Writing mechanics" (or "the mechanics of writing") refers to the technical rules that govern how writing is constructed — spelling, punctuation, capitalization, grammar, and sentence structure. These are distinct from a writer's ideas or style; they are the baseline technical rules every piece of writing must follow to be clear and correct.

In sports: When a coach talks about an athlete's "mechanics," they mean the technical form of a physical action. A golfer's "swing mechanics" means the exact way they position their feet, rotate their hips, and swing the club. A swimmer's "stroke mechanics" means the precise technique of their arm pull and body rotation. Good mechanics = technically sound, efficient form. Poor mechanics = wasteful or injury-prone form.

In games (especially video games): "Game mechanics" refers to the rules, systems, and interactive elements that define how a game is played — how a player earns points, how movement works, how combat is resolved, how resources are gathered. Designers say "the mechanics" to mean the functional rules of play, separate from the game's story, art, or music.

When used this way, "mechanics" is always plural in agreement: "The mechanics of the deal are complex" — not "is."
Meaning 3: More Than One Mechanic (Plural of "Mechanic")

A mechanic (singular noun) is a person who repairs, maintains, or builds machines — most commonly motor vehicles like cars and motorcycles, but also aircraft, industrial equipment, and other machinery. Mechanics is simply the plural form:

  • "Two mechanics spent the afternoon working on the engine."
  • "She trained as one of the first female aircraft mechanics in the country."

This meaning is the most straightforward of the three and rarely causes confusion, since the context almost always makes it clear you're talking about people.

These three meanings aren't random. They share a deep common thread: the functional, operational layer of how something works.

  • The science of mechanics studies how physical things — objects, particles, fluids — operate and move at a fundamental level.
  • "The mechanics of X" describes how any process, system, or skill operates in practical detail.
  • A mechanic is a person whose expertise is understanding and fixing how machines operate.

In every case, "mechanics" points inward — toward the working structure of something, not its surface appearance or its purpose, but the actual functional logic underneath.

Mechanics (noun) — three meanings:

1. The science: The field of physics that studies motion, forces, and energy. It branches into classical mechanics (everyday objects), quantum mechanics (subatomic particles), fluid mechanics (liquids and gases), celestial mechanics (space bodies), and statistical mechanics (linking microscopic to macroscopic behavior). Treated as singular: "Mechanics is..."

2. The workings: "The mechanics of X" = the practical, step-by-step details of how X functions. Used in sports (physical technique), writing (technical rules), games (rules of play), and virtually any other domain. Treated as plural: "The mechanics are..."

3. The people: Simply the plural of mechanic — people who repair and maintain machines.
